def: Restriction enzymes are molecular scissors that cut DNA at specific sequences, and vectors are DNA molecules (like plasmids) used to carry and insert a desired gene into a host cell — both are essential tools of genetic engineering.
points: Restriction enzymes (restriction endonucleases) recognize specific short DNA sequences and cut both strands at that point.
This cutting creates DNA fragments with 'sticky ends' that can join with other DNA cut by the same enzyme.
Example: EcoRI is a commonly used restriction enzyme in recombinant DNA technology.
Vectors are carrier DNA molecules (commonly plasmids or bacteriophages) that transport the foreign gene into a host cell.
A good vector must be able to replicate independently inside the host and should have a marker gene (e.g., antibiotic resistance) to identify successfully transformed cells.
The foreign gene is inserted into the vector using the same restriction enzyme, so their sticky ends match.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Restriction enzyme cuts DNA"] --> B["Sticky ends formed"]
  B --> C["Gene inserted into vector plasmid"]
  C --> D["Recombinant DNA vector ready"]

example: The enzyme EcoRI is used to cut both the foreign gene and the plasmid vector at the same recognition sequence, so their matching sticky ends can join together.
tip: Mention 'sticky ends' and a specific enzyme/vector example by name (EcoRI, plasmid) — naming specifics earns extra marks.

def: Recombinant DNA technology is the process of isolating a gene of interest, combining it with a vector, and introducing it into a host organism so that the host produces the desired protein or trait.
points: Isolation of DNA: the desired gene (DNA of interest) is isolated from the source organism.
Cutting: restriction enzymes cut both the gene and the vector plasmid to create matching sticky ends.
Ligation: the gene is joined to the vector using the enzyme DNA ligase, forming recombinant DNA.
Transformation: the recombinant DNA (vector + gene) is introduced into a host cell (e.g., bacteria).
Selection: host cells that successfully took up the recombinant DNA are identified using marker genes.
Expression and multiplication: the host cell multiplies and expresses the foreign gene, producing the desired protein in bulk.
formula: Isolate gene -> Cut with restriction enzyme -> Ligate into vector -> Transform host -> Select -> Express product

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Isolate gene of interest"] --> B["Cut gene and vector"]
  B --> C["Ligate into recombinant DNA"]
  C --> D["Transform into host cell"]
  D --> E["Select and express product"]

example: Human insulin gene inserted into E. coli bacteria using this technology allows bacteria to mass-produce human insulin for diabetic patients.
tip: Write the steps strictly in order (isolate, cut, ligate, transform, select, express) — sequence matters for full marks in this process-based question.

def: PCR is a laboratory technique used to make millions of copies of a specific DNA segment in a short time, using repeated cycles of heating and cooling with a heat-stable DNA polymerase enzyme.
points: PCR needs: template DNA, primers (short DNA sequences that mark the start points), DNA polymerase (usually Taq polymerase), and nucleotides.
Denaturation: the DNA is heated (around 95°C) to separate the two strands.
Annealing: the mixture is cooled so primers bind (anneal) to the complementary sequences on each strand.
Extension: Taq polymerase extends the primers, synthesizing new complementary DNA strands.
Each cycle doubles the amount of target DNA, so after 'n' cycles the DNA increases exponentially (2^n copies).
PCR is used in DNA fingerprinting, diagnosis of genetic and infectious diseases, and forensic analysis.
formula: Amount of DNA after n cycles = original amount x 2^n

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Denaturation: heat to separate strands"] --> B["Annealing: primers bind"]
  B --> C["Extension: Taq polymerase copies DNA"]
  C --> D["Cycle repeats, DNA doubles each time"]

example: Starting with one DNA molecule, after 10 PCR cycles the DNA amount becomes 2^10 = 1024 copies, enough for further analysis.
tip: Write the three steps (denaturation, annealing, extension) with approximate temperatures — examiners check for correct sequence and terms.

def: Gel electrophoresis is a laboratory technique used to separate DNA fragments (or proteins) of different sizes by making them move through a gel under an electric field.
points: DNA fragments are loaded into wells at one end of an agarose gel.
An electric current is applied; since DNA is negatively charged (due to phosphate groups), it moves toward the positive electrode.
Smaller DNA fragments move faster and travel farther through the gel pores; larger fragments move slower.
This separates DNA fragments by size, forming distinct bands.
The separated DNA bands are visualized using staining (e.g., ethidium bromide) under UV light.
This technique is a key step after PCR or restriction digestion to check the size and purity of DNA fragments.

diagram.draw: Draw a rectangular gel tray with wells at the top (negative electrode side) and the gel body leading to the bottom (positive electrode side). Show sample lanes with bands at different positions: smaller fragments shown as bands nearer the bottom (moved farther), larger fragments as bands near the top (moved less). Label wells, direction of DNA movement, negative and positive electrodes.

example: After a PCR reaction, running the product on gel electrophoresis and comparing it with a DNA ladder confirms the size of the amplified gene fragment.
tip: Clearly state that DNA moves towards the positive electrode because DNA is negatively charged — this reasoning is often specifically asked.

def: Genetically Modified (GM) crops are plants whose genes have been altered using genetic engineering to introduce desirable traits; Bt cotton is a GM crop containing a bacterial gene that makes it resistant to certain insect pests.
points: Bt cotton contains a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that produces a toxin protein (Cry protein) toxic to specific insect larvae like the cotton bollworm.
When the pest insect eats the plant, the toxin damages its gut, killing the insect, while being harmless to humans and other animals.
This reduces the need for chemical pesticides, lowering cost and environmental damage.
Other GM crop examples include Bt brinjal and golden rice (enriched with vitamin A precursor).
GM crops can also be engineered for herbicide tolerance, drought resistance, or improved nutrition.
Concerns about GM crops include possible effects on biodiversity, allergenicity, and need for regulatory approval before release.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Bt gene from Bacillus thuringiensis"] --> B["Inserted into cotton plant genome"]
  B --> C["Plant produces Cry toxin protein"]
  C --> D["Pest insect dies after feeding on plant"]

example: Bt cotton has significantly reduced bollworm damage in Indian cotton fields, cutting down pesticide use and increasing yield.
tip: Name the specific bacterium (Bacillus thuringiensis) and the toxin (Cry protein) — these exact terms are commonly checked.

def: Gene therapy is a technique of correcting a genetic disorder by inserting a normal, functional gene into a patient's cells to replace or supplement a missing or defective gene.
points: It is used to treat genetic disorders caused by a single defective gene, such as ADA deficiency (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, SCID).
A normal copy of the gene is delivered into the patient's cells, often using a modified virus (viral vector) as the carrier.
The inserted gene produces the missing protein or enzyme, correcting the disorder.
Gene therapy can be done ex vivo (cells removed, treated, and reinserted into the body) or in vivo (gene delivered directly into the body).
Besides treating genetic disorders, biotechnology applications include producing hormones (insulin), vaccines, and diagnostic kits.
Gene therapy raises ethical questions and requires careful testing because of safety and long-term effect concerns.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Identify defective gene in patient"] --> B["Normal gene inserted via viral vector"]
  B --> C["Gene enters patient cells"]
  C --> D["Normal protein produced, disorder corrected"]

example: The first approved gene therapy case treated a child with ADA deficiency (SCID) by inserting a functional ADA gene into her blood cells, restoring her immune function.
tip: Give the ADA deficiency/SCID example by name — it is the classic textbook case examiners expect in this topic.
